questions.question: Is the position in the sequence part of the input?

result.answer:
The network takes as input an image I_i from the sequence at every timestep t. [1]
Each decoder's first input is its corresponding image embedding e(I_i), while the context vector initializes each decoder's hidden state. [2]
All five decoders take the corresponding image embedding as their first input. [3]
The decoder's first input x_0 is the image for which the text is being generated. [4]

questions.question: How is the sequential nature of the story captured?

result.answer:
The visual storyteller incorporates a context encoder and multiple independent decoders to generate stories from image sequences. [1]
Each decoder generates a sequence of words for each image in the sequence, and the final story is the concatenation of the output of the 5 decoders. [2]
The decoders are specialized by position: the first decoder learns the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder learns the closing sentences. [3]
The decoder is provided with the context of the whole sequence and the content of the current image (global and local information) to generate the corresponding text contributing to the overall story. [4]

result.answer:
The multilingual model uses word alignments between sentences in a parallel corpus to exploit role correspondences across languages. [1]
Adding word alignments in parallel sentences results in small, non-significant improvements, even when some labeled data is available in the source language. [2]
The multilingual model obtains small improvements in both languages, confirming the standard unsupervised setup results. [3]
The results indicate that little information can be learned about semantic roles from this parallel data setup. [4]
The authors suggest that improving the alignment model is a necessary step to making effective use of parallel data in multilingual SRI. [5]

questions.question: What does an individual model consist of?

result.answer:
The model consists of individual Bayesian models for each language, plus crosslingual latent variables that incorporate soft role agreement between aligned constituents. [1]
The multilingual model is built by making copies of the monolingual model for each language and adding crosslingual latent variables (CLVs) to couple the monolingual models, capturing crosslingual semantic role patterns. [2]

questions.question: What baseline model is used?

result.answer:
The baseline used is the same baseline as used by lang2011unsupervised, which assigns a semantic role to a constituent based on its syntactic function (the dependency relation to its head). [1]
The base monolingual model is the Bayesian model of garg2012unsupervised. [2]

documents.title: GlossBERT: BERT for Word Sense Disambiguation with Gloss Knowledge

questions.question: How does the neural network architecture accomodate an unknown amount of senses per word?

result.answer:
GlossBERT constructs context-gloss pairs from glosses of all possible senses of the target word in WordNet, treating WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem. [1][2]
For each target word, glosses of all N possible senses are extracted to form the gloss sentence; in the given example N=4. [3]
At test time, the probability of label=yes is output for each context-gloss pair, and the sense with the highest probability is chosen as the prediction. [4]

result.answer:
GlossBERT constructs context-gloss pairs from glosses of all possible senses of the target word in WordNet, treating WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem. [1][2]

questions.question: What is the ROUGE score of the highest performing model?

result.answer:
The model reports a 33.33 average of ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L on CNN/Daily Mail, described as state-of-the-art. [1][2]
On CNN/Daily Mail, the reported ROUGE metrics are full-length F-1 scores for ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L. [3]
On NYT50, the evaluation uses limited-length ROUGE recall, with generated summary length limited to the ground-truth length. [4]

result.answer:
Our model achieves a 33.33 average of ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L on the CNN/Daily Mail, which is state-of-the-art. [1][2]
On the New York Times dataset, our model achieves about 5.6% relative improvement over ROUGE-1. [3][4]
Compared to extractive models NeuSUM and MASK-LM^global, our model achieves slightly higher ROUGE-1. [5]
Compared to the ML+RL with intra-attn approach (previous SOTA), our model gets 2.39 ROUGE-1 improvement and 0.51 ROUGE-2 improvement. [6][7]

questions.question: Why masking words in the decoder is helpful?

result.answer:
掩码使精炼解码器在给定摘要其他词的情况下预测第n个精炼词，从而逐词编辑草稿。 [1][2]
该过程与BERT预训练中的完形填空任务相似，因此解码器可利用上下文语言模型的能力生成更流畅、自然的序列。 [3]
从BERT等上下文化嵌入的角度看，精炼解码过程提供了更完整的输入序列，与其预训练过程一致。 [4]
两阶段解码器使模型在生成每个摘要词时能同时考虑两侧的上下文信息。 [5]

questions.question: How are the different components of the model trained? Is it trained end-to-end?

result.answer:
该模型可以端到端训练，无需手工特征。 [1]
模型采用两阶段解码器流程，生成摘要的每个词时会同时考虑两侧上下文信息。 [2]
训练时模型的目标是两个过程之和，使用“teacher-forcing”算法联合训练，并向每个解码器输入真实摘要以最小化目标。 [3]
模型损失为解码器损失与refine损失之和。 [4]
模型变体包括One-Stage（基于BERT的带复制机制的序列到序列模型）、Two-Stage（在One-Stage上增加word-refine解码器）以及Two-Stage + RL（refine过程与RL目标配合的完整模型）。 [5]
训练使用Adam优化器，学习率为3e-4，并在训练过程中使用动态学习率。 [6]
训练时batch size设为36，训练4个epoch（NYT50因训练样本少得多而训练8个epoch），训练后根据开发集表现从最后10个模型中选出最佳模型。 [7]

documents.title: A Hybrid Architecture for Multi-Party Conversational Systems

questions.question: What is the state of the art described in the paper?

result.answer:
The paper states it is not meant to advance the state of the art on the norms for MPCS. [1]
The paper says that, to the best of the authors' knowledge, its proposed architecture is the first in the state of the art designed to support the design and development of coordinated aware chatbots in a multiparty conversation. [2]
The paper describes the state of the art for creating chatbots that can participate in multiparty conversations as currently a combination of research on creating chatbots and research on the coordination or governance of multi-agent systems. [3]
The paper says that in the state of the art, most proposed approaches for context reasoning rely on rules using logics and knowledge bases. [4]
The paper says the most recent state of the art for developing such systems has employed RNNs, Dynamic Context-Sensitive Generation, and Memory Networks, among others. [5]
The paper notes a lack of research directed at building coordination laws integrated with natural language for chatbot engines. [6]
The paper discusses the state of the art on conversational systems from three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning. [7]

result.answer:
论文对对话系统领域现状的综述从三个视角展开：交互类型、架构类型和上下文推理类型，并用一张表进行汇总比较。 [1]
在上下文推理方面，现有大多数方法依赖使用逻辑和知识库的规则。 [2]
对于能够参与多方可对话的聊天机器人的创建，当前现状是聊天机器人创建研究与多智能体系统协调或治理研究的结合。 [3]
开发此类系统的最新现状采用了循环神经网络（RNN）、动态上下文敏感生成和记忆网络等。 [4]
在聊天机器人引擎方面，缺乏将协调法则与自然语言相结合的研究。 [5]
据作者所知，本文提出的架构是现有技术中首个为支持多方可对话中协调感知聊天机器人的设计与开发而设计的架构。 [6]

documents.title: Negated LAMA: Birds cannot fly

questions.question: How did they extend LAMA evaluation framework to focus on negation?

result.answer:
They introduced the negated LAMA dataset, constructed by inserting negation elements (e.g., "not") into LAMA cloze statements. [1]
They focused on factual knowledge stored in negated statements, questioning to what extent such knowledge is indirectly acquired during pretraining. [2][3]
In their experiments, they queried pretrained language models with both original LAMA and negated LAMA statements and compared predictions via rank correlation and overlap of top predictions. [4]
They also created negated versions of Google-RE, T-REx and SQuAD by manually inserting a negation element in each template or statement. [5]

他们通过构建negated LAMA数据集来扩展LAMA评估框架：在LAMA完形填空陈述中插入否定元素（如“not”）。 [1]
他们还通过在每个模板或陈述中手动插入否定元素，创建了Google-RE、T-REx和SQuAD的否定版本。 [2]
在实验中，他们用原始LAMA和否定LAMA陈述查询预训练语言模型，并从排名相关性和前几名预测的重叠两方面比较预测结果。 [3]

documents.title: Character-Level Question Answering with Attention

questions.question: What word level and character level model baselines are used?

result.answer:
The word-level model is explored as an alternative to character-level models for constructing embeddings for questions, entities and predicates. [1]
The word-level model has 19.9M parameters and achieves a best SQ accuracy of 53.9%, compared to the character-level model's 1.2M parameters. [2]
Both word-level and character-level models perform comparably on predicate prediction, reaching around 80% accuracy. [3]
The word-level model generalizes poorly to unseen entities, predicting only 45% of entities accurately from the mixed set, whereas character-level models achieve 96.6% accuracy on the mixed set. [3][4]
The character-level model is described as a character-level, attention-based encoder-decoder model. [5]

questions.question: How are the supervised scores of the words calculated?

result.answer:
The supervised polarity score per word is calculated using the training data only, as given in (DISPLAY_FORM4). [1]
Each value in a row is multiplied by the corresponding row word's raw supervised score. [1]
As an alternative, all row scores were separately multiplied by +1 for a positive row word and by -1 for a negative row word. [2][3]
For a target word, in addition to its self polarity score, the minimum, maximum, and average polarity scores of words in the same contexts are considered. [4][5]

questions.question: Which hand-crafted features are combined with word2vec?

result.answer:
The hand-crafted features combined with word2vec are three supervised polarity scores extracted per review: minimum, mean, and maximum polarity scores. [1][2][3]
These three scores are concatenated to the averaged word vector per review. [3]
Combining unsupervised word vectors with the supervised three scores yielded better state-of-the-art results. [4]

questions.question: What details are given about the Twitter dataset?

result.answer:
One Twitter dataset has nearly 1.6 million tweets annotated through a distant supervised method, with positive, neutral, and negative labels. [1]
A balanced Twitter dataset was generated by randomly selecting 7,020 positive tweets and 7,020 negative tweets. [2]
The Turkish Twitter corpus consists of tweets about Turkish mobile network operators, which are mostly much noisier and shorter than movie reviews. [3]
One Twitter dataset totals 1,716 tweets, of which 973 are negative and 743 are positive. [4]
Success rates for the movie corpus are much better than those for the Twitter dataset for most approaches, since tweets are generally much shorter and noisier. [5]
For the English Twitter dataset, accuracy decreases in some cases when polarity labels are used. [6][7]
When the 3-feats technique is not considered, the corpus-based SVD method yields the highest accuracies for the English Twitter dataset. [8]
Accuracies of about 88 per cent were achieved for the English Twitter dataset. [9]

questions.question: What details are given about the movie domain dataset?

result.answer:
The Turkish movie dataset consists of movie reviews collected from a popular website, with 20,244 reviews and an average of 39 words per review. [1]
An English movie corpus collected from the web was used as one of two additional English datasets to test cross-linguality. [2]
For the movie corpus, 7,020 negative and 7,020 positive reviews were randomly selected and only those were processed. [3]
The models were evaluated on four corpora: the movie and Twitter datasets in Turkish and English, with embeddings learned separately on each. [4]
The TDK dictionary covers most of the domain-specific vocabulary used in the movie reviews, which is why the dictionary method performs well on them. [5]
Success rates for the movie corpus were much better than for the Twitter dataset for most approaches, since tweets are generally much shorter and noisier. [6]
Accuracies of over 90 per cent were achieved for the Turkish movie corpus using an SVM classifier. [7]

questions.question: What semantic and syntactic tasks are used as probes?

result.answer:
Syntactic probes include the Google Syntactic analogies (GSyn) for word-level syntactic information, and the Depth (Dep) and Top Constituent (TopC) probing tasks from SentEval for sentence-level syntax. [1]
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is also used as a syntactic task. [2]
Semantic probes include the Semantic Textual Similarity (STSB) task and the Word Content (WC) probing task from SentEval for sentence-level semantics. [3]
For word-level semantics, the SimLex and Rare Word (RW) word similarity datasets and the Google Semantic (GSem) analogies are used. [4]

questions.question: What approaches do they use towards text analysis?

result.answer:
Computational text analysis is described as an addition to, not a replacement for, other approaches to analyzing social and cultural phenomena using textual data. [1]
The approaches used and the meaning of "success" are guided by the research questions. [2]
Some approaches are effective for prediction but harder to interpret, so the value placed on interpretability can influence the approach chosen. [3]
Recent neural network approaches often use simple features as input, such as word embeddings or character sequences, requiring less feature engineering but making interpretation more difficult. [4]
When using a supervised approach, errors (disagreement between system output and human-provided labels) can point to interesting cases for closer analysis and help reflect on conceptualizations. [5]
Computational analysis of text motivated by these questions is insight driven, aiming to describe a phenomenon or explain how it came about. [6]
For insight-driven text analysis, it is often critical that high-level patterns can be communicated. [7]
A landmark study analyzed the authorship of The Federalist Papers using statistical text analysis focused on style, based on the distribution of function words rather than content. [8]
Tasks mentioned range from core linguistically motivated tasks such as part-of-speech tagging and parsing to filtering spam and detecting sentiment. [9]

documents.title: Context-Aware Monolingual Repair for Neural Machine Translation

questions.question: what was the baseline?

result.answer:
The baseline is described as a context-agnostic MT system; the DocRepair model operates on groups of sentences and can fix consistency errors caused by it. [1][2]
The baseline model is a Transformer base model with N=6 layers and h=8 attention heads, the same architecture as the back-translation model and DocRepair. [3]
For fair comparison with previous work, the baseline MT system was trained on data released by BIBREF11, on 6m instances. [4]
A second baseline used is the two-pass CADec model: the first pass produces sentence-level translations, and the second pass takes the first-pass translation plus context-sentence representations and returns contextualized translations. [5]
The model initially learns to copy baseline translations, with very high BLEU against the baseline, then gradually changes them. [6]
The BLEU score between translations of the converged model and the baseline is 82.5. [7]
DocRepair outperforms the baseline and CADec by 0.7 BLEU, and its sentence-level repair version by 0.5 BLEU. [8]

questions.question: what phenomena do they mention is hard to capture?

result.answer:
The records state that discourse phenomena are hard to capture using monolingual data only, but they do not name the specific phenomena in that general statement. [1][2][3]
Among the four phenomena in the test sets (deixis, lexical cohesion, VP ellipsis, and ellipsis affecting NP inflection), VP ellipsis is identified as the hardest phenomenon to capture using round-trip translations. [4][5][6]
The records hypothesize that this is because it is hard to learn to correct inconsistencies in translations caused by VP ellipsis relying on monolingual data alone. [7]

questions.question: How was the spatial aspect of the EEG signal computed?

result.answer:
The spatial aspect was addressed by computing the channel cross-covariance, producing positive semi-definite matrices that encode the connectivity of the electrodes, rather than selecting a handful of channels. [1]
Spatial connections between electrodes were decoded from the channel covariance matrix using a four-layered 2D CNN with two convolutional and two fully connected hidden layers. [2]
The CNN and LSTM were combined to provide a more powerful discriminative spatial and temporal representation than either network alone. [3]
The last fully connected layer of the CNN was concatenated with its counterpart in the LSTM to form a single feature vector. [4]

questions.question: Does their NER model learn NER from both text and images?

result.answer:
Their proposed LSTM-CNN hybrid multimodal NER network takes both image and text as input to recognize named entities in text input. [1]
Their MNER model obtains word embeddings, character embeddings, and visual features, with each input token composed of word, character, and visual embeddings. [2][3]
They demonstrated an effective MNER system in which visual information is combined with textual information to outperform traditional text-based NER baselines. [4]

questions.question: Do they inspect their model to see if their model learned to associate image parts with words related to entities?

result.answer:
The paper reports that the image-aided model (W+C+V) uses modality attention to attenuate irrelevant signals (e.g., selfies) and amplify relevant modality-based contexts when predicting a token. [1]
The paper states that visual contexts help disambiguate polysemous tokens, such as predicting 'Apple' as a fruit rather than an organization, and 'monopoly' as a named entity. [2][3]
The paper reports that visual contexts (visual tags such as 'parade' and 'urban area') provide similarities to a token's distributional semantics from other training examples, and the model then successfully predicts the token as a named entity. [4]

questions.question: Which text embedding methodologies are used?

result.answer:
The framework uses fixed-sized vector embeddings (Doc2Vec) rather than standard bag of words (BoW). [1]
A Doc2Vec model is used to infer high-dimensional vector descriptions for the text of each of the 3229 documents in the target analysis set. [2]
The approach combines recently developed deep neural-network high-dimensional text-embedding algorithms with network-theoretical methods. [3]
The framework combines text-embedding, geometric graph construction and multi-resolution community detection. [4]
The text embedding was trained on 13 million records collected by the NRLS since 2004, although a much smaller corpus can be used. [5]

result.answer:
该框架使用文本嵌入（text-embedding），并结合几何图构建与多分辨率社区检测。 [1][2]

该Doc2Vec模型用于为3229份文档的文本推断高维向量描述。 [4]
方法结合了近期开发的深度神经网络高维文本嵌入算法与网络理论方法。 [5]

supportQuotes.quote: Our framework combines text-embedding, geometric graph construction and multi-resolution community detection to identify, rather than impose, content-based clusters from free, unstructured text in an unsupervised manner.

Our framework combines text-embedding, geometric graph construction and multi-resolution community detection to identify, rather than impose, content-based clusters from free, unstructured text in an unsupervised manner.

claims.text: 该框架使用文本嵌入（text-embedding），并结合几何图构建与多分辨率社区检测。

supportQuotes.quote: The use of fixed-sized vector embeddings (Doc2Vec) instead of standard bag of words (BoW) is an integral part of our pipeline.

claims.text: 使用固定大小的向量嵌入（Doc2Vec），而非标准词袋（BoW）。

supportQuotes.quote: This Doc2Vec model is subsequently used to infer high-dimensional vector descriptions for the text of each of the 3229 documents in our target analysis set.

claims.text: 该Doc2Vec模型用于为3229份文档的文本推断高维向量描述。

supportQuotes.quote: To do so, we combine recently developed deep neural-network high-dimensional text-embedding algorithms with network-theoretical methods.

claims.text: 方法结合了近期开发的深度神经网络高维文本嵌入算法与网络理论方法。

supportQuotes.quote: First, we use the 13 million records collected by the NRLS since 2004 to train our text embedding (although a much smaller corpus can be used).

result.answer:
The features polarity, POS and NER, when introduced in LSTM-CRF, improve F1. [1]
The LSTM-CRF mode uses word embeddings and character embeddings plus token-level features such as polarity, POS and NER. [2]
The paper reports gains in performance due to the features, ensemble schemes, multi-tasking and multi-granularity architectures. [3]

questions.question: What is specific to multi-granularity and multi-tasking neural arhiteture design?

result.answer:
The work reports performance gains attributable to features, ensemble schemes, multi-tasking and multi-granularity architectures. [1]
A multi-granularity network based on LSTM-CRF and BERT was used to investigate performing FLC and SLC jointly. [2]
The LSTM-CRF+Multi-grain model jointly performs FLC and SLC with FastTextWordEmb and BERTSentEmb respectively, adding a binary sentence classification loss to sequence tagging weighted by a factor of α. [3]
In the multi-granularity loss, α was set to 0.1 for sentence classification based on dev (internal, fold1) scores. [4]
Multi-tasking was performed with another auxiliary task of PFD. [5]
The LSTM-CRF+Multi-task model performs propagandistic span/fragment detection (PFD) and FLC (fragment detection + 19-way classification). [6]
A multi-task neural sequence tagger based on LSTM-CRF and linguistic features was designed to jointly detect propagandistic fragments and their type. [7]
Multi-grained LSTM-CRF was run without BERTSentEmb and with it; the latter improved scores on dev (internal) but not on dev (external). [8]

questions.question: Does BERT reach the best performance among all the algorithms compared?

result.answer:
BERT does not reach the best performance among all compared algorithms: it remains only 0.3 F1-score points behind and would have achieved the second position among all the MEDDOCAN shared task competitors. [1]
BERT achieves a precision lower than the rest of the systems, making more false positive predictions, but obtains a remarkably higher recall. [2]
In the comparison, the CRF classifier is the most precise of all, and BERT outperforms both the CRF and spaCy classifiers thanks to its greater recall. [3]

questions.question: What are the clinical datasets used in the paper?

result.answer:
The experiments are carried out on two datasets: the MEDDOCAN Medical Document Anonymization shared task dataset and NUBes, a corpus of real medical reports in Spanish. [1]
One experiment uses the MEDDOCAN 2019 shared task dataset, while the other uses a novel Spanish clinical reports dataset called NUBes-PHI. [2]
Both datasets consist of plain text containing clinical narrative written in Spanish, with manual annotations of sensitive information in BRAT standoff format. [3]
The MEDDOCAN shared task organisers curated a synthetic corpus of clinical cases enriched with sensitive information by health documentalists. [4]

questions.question: How is the vocabulary of word-like or phoneme-like units automatically discovered?

result.answer:
Unsupervised term discovery (UTD) based on raw acoustic features aims to identify and cluster repeating word-like units across speech using segmental dynamic time warping (DTW). [1]
UTD automatically identifies and clusters repeated terms (e.g., words or phrases) from speech. [2]
Word repetitions are identified via fast diagonal line search and segmental DTW. [3]
A model-based alternative for producing speech tokenizations without language dependency is unsupervised learning of HMM-based phoneme-like units from untranscribed speech. [4]
In a phone-loop model, each phoneme-like unit is modeled as an HMM with a Gaussian mixture model of output densities (GMM-HMM). [5]
After thresholding the graph edges, each connected component of the graph is a cluster of acoustic segments, producing a corresponding term (word/phrase) category. [6]
The cluster of each discovered term category consists of a list of term occurrences. [7]

result.answer:
UTD（无监督术语发现）从语音中自动识别并聚类重复的词或短语等术语。 [1][2]
UTD通过快速对角线搜索和分段DTW识别词重复，并利用ZRTools中的可扩展UTD框架避免穷举DTW搜索。 [3][4]
对图边做阈值处理后，图的每个连通分量是一簇声学片段，对应一个术语（词/短语）类别；每个已发现术语类别的簇由术语出现列表组成。 [5][6]
另一种不依赖语言的语音标记化方式是模型方法，即从无转写语音中无监督学习基于HMM的音素类单元；phone-loop模型中每个音素类单元被建模为带GMM输出密度的HMM。 [7][8]

questions.question: What experiments are conducted?

result.answer:
Additional experiments were conducted on the transformation from ironic sentences to non-ironic sentences. [1]
Automatic evaluations were also conducted for this transformation, with conclusions similar to those for the transformation from non-ironic sentences to ironic sentences. [2]
During the experiments, some outputs were observed to prefer repeating the same word. [3][4]

questions.question: What are the difficulties in modelling the ironic pattern?

result.answer:
The paper states that there has been little work trying to generate ironies based on the seq2seq framework, attributing this to the lack of a large irony dataset and the difficulties of modeling ironies. [1]
The paper notes that many non-ironic sentences do not have specific stylistic words, making it difficult in practice to transfer non-ironic sentences to ironic sentences by separating content and style through removing stylistic words. [2][3]
The paper observes that not all non-ironic sentences are suitable to be transferred into ironic sentences. [4]
The paper states that the transformation from non-ironic to ironic sentences must preserve sentiment polarity, unlike other style-transfer studies. [5]
The paper notes that in figurative language such as irony, the sentiment polarity of the literal meaning may differ significantly from that of the intended figurative meaning. [6]
The paper states that the style-independent content representation is not easily obtained, which results in poor performances. [7]
The paper notes that sometimes ironies are hard to understand and may cause misunderstanding. [8]

questions.question: What dataset is used to train the model?

result.answer:
The sentiment analyzer was trained using 3,216 tweets. [1]
The machine learning model for classifying non-human annotated tweets was trained with features extracted from the human annotated tweets. [2]
The features extracted from the human annotated tweets were fed to the classifier and trained using the random forest algorithm. [3]
The classifier using Word2vec representations of human annotated tweets was trained on the Random Forest algorithm with a 90% training split. [4]
The model trained with word2vec representations was selected to classify the non-human annotated tweets. [5]

questions.question: How was annotation performed?

result.answer:
Annotation was performed using WebAnno, a web-based tool for linguistic annotation; annotators could choose between a pre-annotated version or a blank version of each text. [1]
The annotation was manual, covering all mentions of case entities, conditions, findings, factors and modifiers, limited to the presentation of a patient's signs and symptoms. [2]
Following a pilot annotation phase, two different annotators annotated two case reports according to the guidelines, and the same annotators annotated an overall collection of 53 case reports. [3]

documents.title: Shallow Syntax in Deep Water

questions.question: Does this method help in sentiment classification task improvement?

result.answer:
On sentiment classification, chunk features are slightly harmful on average, though variance is high. [1]
mSynC performs similarly to ELMo-transformer on sentiment classification. [1]
Overall, performance differences across all tasks are small enough to infer that shallow syntax is not particularly helpful when using cwrs. [2]
Exposing cwr-based models to shallow syntax, via new architectures or explicit pipelined features, has little effect on their performance across several tasks. [3]

questions.question: What are improvements for these two approaches relative to ELMo-only baselines?

result.answer:
In both settings, the work observes only modest gains on three of the four downstream tasks relative to ELMo-only baselines. [1][2]
Shallow syntactic features offer little to no benefit to ELMo models, though they are helpful to span-level task models without cwrs. [3]
Explicit shallow syntax does not offer any benefits over ELMo-transformer. [4]
On sentiment classification, chunk features are slightly harmful on average (with high variance), and mSynC performs similarly to ELMo-transformer. [5]
mSynC performs slightly worse than the ELMo-transformer baseline on 7 out of 9 tasks. [6]
On the chunk-tag probe, mSynC achieves 96.9 F1 versus 92.2 F1 for ELMo-transformer, indicating mSynC encodes shallow syntax. [7]
The shallow-syntax-aware contextual embeddings do not transfer to linguistic tasks any more easily than ELMo embeddings. [8]

questions.question: What traditional linguistics features did they use?

result.answer:
The authors state they augmented traditional linguistic features with cognitive features from readers' eye-movement data, in the form of simple gaze-based features and complex features derived from a graph structure. [1]
Prior sarcasm-detection work is described as using distant supervision techniques (e.g., hashtags) and stylistic/pragmatic features such as emoticons and laughter expressions like “lol.” [2]
Computational linguists are described as using rule-based and statistical techniques with unigrams and pragmatic features, stylistic patterns, situational-disparity patterns, and hashtag interpretations. [3]
The paper's feature set labeled “Sarcasm” is the feature-set reported by joshi2015harnessing, subsuming unigram features and features from other reported systems. [4]

questions.question: What language model architectures are used?

result.answer:
The work considers two types of architectures: a bi-directional language model to augment the sequence to sequence encoder and a uni-directional model to augment the decoder. [1]
The experiments rely on strong transformer-based language models trained on up to six billion tokens. [2]
The approach augments a standard sequence to sequence model with pre-trained representations following an ELMo-style regime as well as by fine-tuning the language model. [3]

documents.title: Dice Loss for Data-imbalanced NLP Tasks

questions.question: How are weights dynamically adjusted?

result.answer:
The authors propose a dynamic weight adjusting strategy, inspired by focal loss, that associates each training example with a weight proportional to (1-p); this weight changes dynamically as training proceeds. [1]
The strategy deemphasizes confident examples as their p approaches 1, making the model attentive to hard-negative examples and alleviating the dominating effect of easy-negative examples. [2]
(1-p_i1) can be viewed as a weight associated with each example that changes as training proceeds; changing p_i1 to (1-p_i1)p_i1 pushes down the weight of easy examples. [3]
For easy examples whose probability approaches 0 or 1, (1-p_i1)p_i1 makes the model attach significantly less focus to them. [4]
Other works (BIBREF23, BIBREF24) adjusted the weights of different training examples based on training loss. [5]
In self-paced learning, example weights are obtained by optimizing the weighted training loss, which encourages learning easier examples first; at each training step the algorithm optimizes model parameters and example weights jointly. [6][7]
Importance sampling assigns weights to different samples and changes the data distribution. [8]
Recent work proposed learning a separate network to predict sample weights. [9]
Focal loss down-weights the loss assigned to well-classified examples by adding a (1-p)^β factor, giving final loss (1-p)^β log p. [10]

result.answer:
本文提出的动态权重调整策略为每个训练样本关联一个与(1-p)成正比的权重，该权重随训练过程动态变化。 [1]
该策略在样本的p接近1时降低对高置信样本的重视，使模型关注难负样本，从而缓解简单负样本的主导作用。 [2]
可将(1-p_{i1})视为每个样本的权重，它随训练进行而变化；将p_{i1}改为(1-p_{i1})p_{i1}的直觉是压低简单样本的权重。 [3]
对于概率接近0或1的简单样本，(1-p_{i1})p_{i1}使模型对其关注显著减少。 [4]

questions.question: What is the attention module pretrained on?

result.answer:
The proposed method reuses the pre-trained MT attention module in ST, leveraging alignment information learned in pre-training. [1]
The attention module is task-specific; in the many-to-many multi-task model, three attentions are defined. [2][3]
Previous work trains attention modules for ASR, MT and ST respectively, so the ST attention module does not benefit from pre-training. [4]

questions.question: What are the baselines?

result.answer:
The paper compares its method with several baselines, including a vanilla ST baseline that has only a speech encoder and a decoder and is trained from scratch on the ST-TED corpus. [1][2]
Three multi-task baseline experiments are conducted: one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many settings. [3]
Three pre-training baseline experiments are conducted: encoder pre-training (ST encoder initialized from an ASR model), decoder pre-training (ST decoder initialized from an MT model), and encoder-decoder pre-training. [4]
A cascaded system baseline is built by combining the ASR model and MT model used in the pre-training baseline. [5]
Several competitive baselines are reproduced based on ESPnet for a fair comparison. [6]
A `triangle+pretrain' baseline is mentioned, in which a performance degradation is observed. [7]
A strong `many-to-many+pretrain' baseline is mentioned. [8]
